claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claims.claim: Mice injected with DBT-Luc-DGCs alone developed substantially small tumors.
claims.source: As expected, mice injected with DBT-Luc-DGCs alone developed substantially small tumors (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 2C and D.

claims.claim: Small tumors formed in animals injected with either DBT-Luc-GSC+DBT-Luc-DGC/miRFMOD (Dox+) or DBT-Luc-GSC alone expressed significantly less FMOD protein than other tumors.
claims.source: The small tumors formed in animals injected with either DBT-Luc-GSC+DBT-Luc-DGC/miRFMOD (Dox+) or DBT-Luc-GSC alone expressed significantly less FMOD protein than other tumors (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: FMOD secreted by DGCs is essential for the growth of tumors initiated by GSCs.
claims.source: These results indicate that FMOD secreted by DGCs is essential for the growth of tumors initiated by GSCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from co-implantation experiments showing reduced tumor growth when FMOD is silenced in DGCs.

claims.claim: Small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as FMOD promote angiogenesis in the context of cutaneous wound healing.
claims.source: Small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as FMOD promote angiogenesis in the context of cutaneous wound healing (Pang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Pang et al., 2019 and Zheng et al., 2014.

claims.claim: There is significant enrichment of the term 'angiogenesis' among differentially regulated genes in FMOD-silenced U251 glioma cells.
claims.source: In addition, we previously found a significant enrichment of the term 'angiogenesis' among differentially regulated genes in FMOD-silenced U251 glioma cells (Mondal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Conditioned medium from LN229 cells stably expressing FMOD induces more angiogenesis than LN229/Vector stable cells.
claims.source: We found that the CM derived from LN229 cells stably expressing FMOD (LN229/FMOD) induced more angiogenesis than LN229/Vector stable cells (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3A and B.

claims.claim: Conditioned medium of FMOD-silenced U251 cells is less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of cells expressing nontargeting siRNA or shRNA.
claims.source: Further, the CM of FMOD-silenced U251 cells was less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of cells expressing nontargeting siRNA (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or shRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Addition of recombinant human FMOD to the CM of U251/siFMOD cells rescues its ability to induce angiogenesis.
claims.source: The addition of recombinant human FMOD (rhFMOD) to the CM of U251/siFMOD cells rescued its ability to induce angiogenesis (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Addition of rhFMOD directly to endothelial cells induces angiogenesis in the presence of a control antibody (IgG) but not in the presence of an FMOD neutralizing antibody.
claims.source: More importantly, the addition of rhFMOD directly to endothelial cells induced angiogenesis in the presence of a control antibody (IgG) but not in the presence of an FMOD neutralizing antibody ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Conditioned media derived from three DGCs and their corresponding GSCs induce angiogenesis efficiently.
claims.source: Both CMs derived from three DGCs and their corresponding GSCs also induced angiogenesis efficiently (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Pretreating cells with an FMOD antibody significantly reduces the ability of MGG8-DGC CM, but not that of MGG8-GSC CM, to induce angiogenesis.
claims.source: Further, pretreating cells with an FMOD antibody significantly reduced the ability of MGG8-DGC CM, but not that of MGG8-GSC CM, to induce angiogenesis (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The reduced ability of FMOD antibody-pretreated DGC CM to promote angiogenesis is rescued by the exogenous addition of an excess of rhFMOD.
claims.source: The reduced ability of the FMOD antibody-pretreated DGC CM to promote angiogenesis was rescued by the exogenous addition of an excess of rhFMOD (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: CM derived from FMOD-silenced MGG8-DGCs is less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of shNT or siNT transfected MGG-DGCs.
claims.source: Moreover, CM derived from FMOD-silenced MGG8-DGCs was less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of shNT (Figure 3D) or siNT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) transfected MGG-DGCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The effect of FMOD silencing on angiogenesis is rescued by adding exogenous rhFMOD.
claims.source: The effect of FMOD silencing was rescued by adding exogenous rhFMOD (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Both rhFMOD and FMOD present in the CM collected from MGG8-DGC induce the migration and invasion but not the proliferation of ST1 cells.
claims.source: Both rhFMOD and FMOD present in the CM collected from MGG8-DGC induced the migration and invasion but not the proliferation of ST1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Boyden chamber migration and invasion assays and MTT proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-E.

claims.claim: CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells is more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by human brain-derived primary endothelial cells (HBMECs).
claims.source: Further, CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells was more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by human brain-derived primary endothelial cells (HBMECs) and mouse brain-derived immortalized endothelial cells (B.End3) (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3E and F.

claims.claim: CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells is more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by mouse brain-derived immortalized endothelial cells (B.End3).
claims.source: Further, CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells was more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by human brain-derived primary endothelial cells (HBMECs) and mouse brain-derived immortalized endothelial cells (B.End3) (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: The effect of FMOD silencing on angiogenesis by HBMECs and B.End3 cells is rescued by adding rhFMOD.
claims.source: Again, the effect of FMOD silencing was rescued by adding rhFMOD (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: Vascular mimicry is one of the alternative mechanisms of angiogenesis wherein tumor-derived endothelial cells (TDECs) originate from GBM cells.
claims.source: Vascular mimicry (VM) is one of the alternative mechanisms of angiogenesis wherein tumor-derived endothelial cells (TDECs) originate from GBM cells (Angara et al., 2017; Ricci-Vitiani et al., 2010; Soda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Angara et al., 2017; Ricci-Vitiani et al., 2010; and Soda et al., 2011.

claims.claim: MGG8-DGC/shNT cells grown in endothelial media under hypoxia differentiate to TDECs as evidenced by an increase in CD31.
claims.source: MGG8-DGC/shNT cells grown in endothelial media (M199) under hypoxia (1% O2) differentiated to TDECS as evidenced by an increase in CD31 (Figure 3G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claims.claim: MGG8-DGC/shFMOD also differentiate to form TDECs, albeit with less efficiency than MGG8-DGC/shNT.
claims.source: MGG8-DGC/shFMOD also differentiated to form TDECs, albeit with less efficiency (Figure 3G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claims.claim: Addition of rhFMOD induces both MGG8-DGC/shNT-TDEC and MGG8-DGC/shFMOD-TDEC cells to form angiogenic networks efficiently.
claims.source: Further, the addition of rhFMOD induced both MGG8-DGC/shNT-TDEC and MGG8-DGC/shFMOD-TDEC cells to form angiogenic networks efficiently (Figure 3I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3I and J.

claims.claim: U87 cells differentiate to TDECs.
claims.source: Similarly, U87 cells differentiated to TDECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A B), which readily formed angiogenic networks in the presence of rhFMOD (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claims.claim: U87-derived TDECs readily form angiogenic networks in the presence of rhFMOD.
claims.source: Similarly, U87 cells differentiated to TDECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A B), which readily formed angiogenic networks in the presence of rhFMOD (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D.

claims.claim: DGC CM can induce angiogenesis.
claims.source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that DGC CM can induce angiogenesis and identify FMOD as a critical mediator of DGC-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple in vitro angiogenesis assay results showing DGC CM induces angiogenesis.

claims.claim: FMOD is a critical mediator of DGC-induced angiogenesis.
claims.source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that DGC CM can induce angiogenesis and identify FMOD as a critical mediator of DGC-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing FMOD silencing or neutralization reduces DGC CM-induced angiogenesis, which is rescued by adding rhFMOD.

claims.claim: A total of 12 proteins exhibit differential abundance in a time-dependent manner in rhFMOD-treated ST1 endothelial cells.
claims.source: A total of 12 proteins exhibited differential abundance in a time-dependent manner in rhFMOD-treated ST1 endothelial cells (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RPPA data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: HES1 is a downstream target of the Notch signaling pathway that has been shown to promote angiogenesis.
claims.source: These include HES1, a downstream target of the Notch signaling pathway that has been shown to promote angiogenesis (Zhao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Zhao et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Addition of rhFMOD induces luciferase activity of Notch-dependent CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters in ST1 cells but not in gamma-secretase inhibitor (GSI) pretreated cells.
claims.source: The addition of rhFMOD induced luciferase activity of Notch-dependent CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters in ST1 cells but not in gamma-secretase inhibitor (GSI; a Notch pathway inhibitor) pretreated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Addition of rhFMOD increases HES1 mRNA and protein levels in ST1 cells, an effect abolished by GSI pretreatment of cells.
claims.source: The addition of rhFMOD also increased HES1 mRNA and protein levels in ST1 cells, an effect abolished by GSI pretreatment of cells (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 4B and C.

claims.claim: rhFMOD treatment results in the translocation of NICD from the cytosol to the nucleus.
claims.source: rhFMOD treatment also resulted in the translocation of NICD (Notch intracellular domain) from the cytosol to the nucleus, as shown by subcellular fractionation and confocal microscopy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: rhFMOD fails to induce angiogenic network formation by GSI-pretreated ST1 cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, rhFMOD failed to induce angiogenic network formation by GSI-pretreated ST1 cells (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: ST1 cells having a stable expression of NICD show enhanced angiogenic network formation than ST1 vector stable cells.
claims.source: In addition, ST1 cells having a stable expression of NICD (ST1/NICD) showed enhanced angiogenic network formation than ST1 vector stable (ST1/Vector) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D.

claims.claim: FMOD present in CM from MGG8-DGCs induces ST1/Vector cells, but not ST1/NICD cells, to form more angiogenic networks.
claims.source: FMOD present in CM from MGG8-DGCs induced ST1/Vector cells, but not ST1/NICD cells, to form more angiogenic networks, suggesting that Notch activation in endothelial cells is an essential step in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: Notch activation in endothelial cells is an essential step in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.source: FMOD present in CM from MGG8-DGCs induced ST1/Vector cells, but not ST1/NICD cells, to form more angiogenic networks, suggesting that Notch activation in endothelial cells is an essential step in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing GSI inhibits FMOD-induced angiogenesis and NICD overexpression enhances angiogenesis independently of FMOD.

claims.claim: RPPA data shows upregulation of pFAK in rhFMOD-treated endothelial cells.
claims.source: The increase in phosphorylated FAK (pFAK, FAK_Py397-R-V; the molecule downstream of integrin signaling) levels in rhFMOD-treated endothelial cells, as shown by RPPA (Figure 4A), also suggested a possible role of integrin signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RPPA data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: FMOD activates integrin signaling via type I collagen to engage the FAK-Src-Rho-ROCK pathway and promote the migration of glioma cells.
claims.source: This is consistent with our previous findings indicating that FMOD activates integrin signaling via type I collagen to engage the FAK-Src-Rho-ROCK pathway and promote the migration of glioma cells (Mondal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Addition of rhFMOD increases pFAK in ST1 cells, but not in cells pretreated with RGD peptide.
claims.source: We first confirmed the activation of integrin signaling by FMOD, as assessed by increased pFAK in rhFMOD-treated ST1 cells, but not in cells pretreated with RGD peptide, an integrin inhibitor (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Addition of RGD peptide inhibits angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM.
claims.source: The addition of RGD peptide inhibited angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM is completely inhibited when ST1 cells are pretreated with inhibitors of FAK or Src.
claims.source: Likewise, angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM was completely inhibited when ST1 cells were pretreated with inhibitors of FAK (FAKi) or Src (PP2), two signaling molecules downstream of integrin (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: FAK and Src inhibitor treatments strongly reduce the basal level of angiogenesis elicited by the CM of LN229/Vector cells.
claims.source: These treatments also strongly reduced the basal level of angiogenesis elicited by the CM of LN229/Vector cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: An inactive analog of Src inhibitor (PP3), as well as inhibitors of RAC1 and ROCK, fail to inhibit the ability of CM derived from LN229/FMOD cells to induce angiogenesis.
claims.source: In contrast, an inactive analog of Src inhibitor (PP3), as well as inhibitors of RAC1 and ROCK, failed to inhibit the ability of CM derived from LN229/FMOD cells to induce angiogenesis (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The interaction of FMOD with type I collagen is essential for integrin activation.
claims.source: Our previous report also demonstrated that the interaction of FMOD with type I collagen is essential for integrin activation (Mondal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The C-terminal region of FMOD comprises 11 leucine-rich-repeats (LRRs), of which the 11th repeat binds to type I collagen.
claims.source: The C-terminal region of FMOD comprises 11 leucine-rich-repeats (LRRs), of which the 11th repeat binds to type I collagen (Oldberg et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Oldberg et al., 2007.

claims.claim: A synthetic interfering peptide (RLDGNEIKR) corresponding to the 11th LRR of type 1 collagen, but not a modified peptide (RLDGNQIMR), competes with rhFMOD for binding to type I collagen to activate integrin signaling in glioma cells.
claims.source: A synthetic interfering peptide (RLDGNEIKR) corresponding to the 11thh LRR of type 1 collagen, but not a modified peptide (RLDGNQIMR), competes with rhFMOD for binding to type I collagen to activate integrin signaling in glioma cells (Mondal et al., 2017; Oldberg et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017 and Oldberg et al., 2007.

claims.claim: rhFMOD-induced luciferase activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc and angiogenesis by ST1 cells are significantly inhibited by the interfering peptide, but not the modified peptide.
claims.source: Consistent with these findings, rhFMOD-induced luciferase activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A B) and angiogenesis by ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C) were significantly inhibited by the interfering peptide, but not the modified peptide, suggesting a crucial role of type I collagen-dependent activation of integrin signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay and in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-C.

claims.claim: Type I collagen-dependent activation of integrin signaling plays a crucial role in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.source: Consistent with these findings, rhFMOD-induced luciferase activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A B) and angiogenesis by ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C) were significantly inhibited by the interfering peptide, but not the modified peptide, suggesting a crucial role of type I collagen-dependent activation of integrin signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing that a peptide that competes with FMOD for binding to type I collagen inhibits FMOD-induced angiogenesis.

claims.claim: Silencing either ITGA6, ITGB1, or ITGAV in ST1 cells significantly reduces the ability of rhFMOD to activate integrin as assessed by reduced pFAK levels.
claims.source: Silencing either of the selected three integrin subunits in ST1 cells reduced significantly the ability of rhFMOD to activate integrin as assessed by reduced pFAK levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–I), thus demonstrating the involvement of αv/β1 and α6/β1 heterodimeric integrin receptors in FMOD activation of integrin signaling in endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-I.

claims.claim: αv/β1 and α6/β1 heterodimeric integrin receptors are involved in FMOD activation of integrin signaling in endothelial cells.
claims.source: Silencing either of the selected three integrin subunits in ST1 cells reduced significantly the ability of rhFMOD to activate integrin as assessed by reduced pFAK levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–I), thus demonstrating the involvement of αv/β1 and α6/β1 heterodimeric integrin receptors in FMOD activation of integrin signaling in endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing that silencing ITGA6, ITGB1, or ITGAV reduces FMOD-induced integrin activation.

claims.claim: Pretreatment of ST1 cells with RGD peptide significantly reduces rhFMOD-elicited CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activation.
claims.source: Pretreatment of ST1 cells with RGD peptide significantly reduced rhFMOD-elicited CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: Pretreatment of cells with FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, significantly reduces rhFMOD-induced CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activity in ST1 cells.
claims.source: Likewise, pretreatment of cells with FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, significantly reduced rhFMOD-induced CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activity in ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D.

claims.claim: rhFMOD fails to increase HES1 transcript and protein levels in ST1 cells treated with either RGD peptide, FAKi, or PP2, but not in cells treated with PP3.
claims.source: Further, rhFMOD failed to increase HES1 transcript and protein levels in ST1 cells treated with either RGD peptide, FAKi, or PP2, but not in cells treated with PP3 (Figure 4G and H, Figure 4—figure supplement 4E–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 4G and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 4E-H.

claims.claim: Addition of rhFMOD induces DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells.
claims.source: While the addition of rhFMOD induced DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells, RGD peptide pretreatment abolished JAG1 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A), suggesting that JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: RGD peptide pretreatment abolishes JAG1 induction by rhFMOD in ST1 cells.
claims.source: While the addition of rhFMOD induced DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells, RGD peptide pretreatment abolished JAG1 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A), suggesting that JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule between integrin and Notch signaling in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
claims.source: While the addition of rhFMOD induced DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells, RGD peptide pretreatment abolished JAG1 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A), suggesting that JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing JAG1 is induced by FMOD in an integrin-dependent manner.

claims.claim: Pretreatment of cells with either FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, abolishes the ability of rhFMOD to induce JAG1 transcript in ST1 cells.
claims.source: Consistently, pretreatment of cells with either FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, also abolished the ability of rhFMOD to induce JAG1 transcript in ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B and C.

claims.claim: JAG1 silencing significantly decreases rhFMOD-induced activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters and HES1 transcript/protein levels in ST1 cells.
claims.source: Further, JAG1 silencing significantly decreased rhFMOD-induced activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters and HES1 transcript/protein levels in ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5D E, Figure 4I–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay, RT-qPCR, and Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5D and E and Figures 4I-K.

claims.claim: JAG1 silencing abolishes the ability of rhFMOD to induce angiogenic networks by ST1 cells.
claims.source: JAG1 silencing also abolished the ability of rhFMOD to induce angiogenic networks by ST1 cells (Figure 4L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4L.

claims.claim: rhFMOD induces the transcript levels of KLF8, a FAK-inducible transcription factor in ST1 cells, but not in RGD peptide pretreated cells.
claims.source: In addition, rhFMOD induced the transcript levels of KLF8, a FAK-inducible transcription factor in ST1 cells, but not in RGD peptide pretreated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5F.

claims.claim: KLF8 silencing in ST1 cells significantly reduces the ability of rhFMOD to increase JAG1 level.
claims.source: Further, KLF8 silencing in ST1 cells significantly reduced the ability of rhFMOD to increase JAG1 level (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G H), suggesting that KLF8 activates JAG1 through an integrin-dependent pathway in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5G and H.

claims.claim: KLF8 activates JAG1 through an integrin-dependent pathway in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
claims.source: Further, KLF8 silencing in ST1 cells significantly reduced the ability of rhFMOD to increase JAG1 level (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G H), suggesting that KLF8 activates JAG1 through an integrin-dependent pathway in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing KLF8 is induced by FMOD in an integrin-dependent manner and KLF8 silencing reduces JAG1 induction by FMOD.

claims.claim: JAG1 is a molecular link between integrin and Notch signaling pathways in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
claims.source: Collectively, these results identify JAG1 as a molecular link between integrin and Notch signaling pathways in FMOD-treated endothelial cells and demonstrate a key role of integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing JAG1 is induced by FMOD via integrin-FAK signaling and JAG1 is required for FMOD-induced Notch activation and angiogenesis.

claims.claim: Integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling plays a key role in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.source: Collectively, these results identify JAG1 as a molecular link between integrin and Notch signaling pathways in FMOD-treated endothelial cells and demonstrate a key role of integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing each component of this pathway is required for FMOD-induced angiogenesis.

claims.claim: There is significant upregulation of transcript levels of FMOD, JAG1, and HES1 in GBM from various datasets.
claims.source: We found a significant upregulation of transcript levels of FMOD, JAG1, and HES1 in GBM from various datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 6A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of multiple publicly available GBM transcriptome datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A-C.

claims.claim: There is a positive correlation between FMOD and HES1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed.
claims.source: We also found a positive correlation between FMOD and HES1 transcripts and between FMOD and JAG1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 6D E), which further substantiates the functional link between FMOD, JAG1, and HES1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of multiple publicly available GBM transcriptome datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6D and E.

claims.claim: There is a positive correlation between FMOD and JAG1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed.
claims.source: We also found a positive correlation between FMOD and HES1 transcripts and between FMOD and JAG1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 6D E), which further substantiates the functional link between FMOD, JAG1, and HES1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of multiple publicly available GBM transcriptome datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6D and E.

claims.claim: High FMOD transcript levels are associated with poor prognosis in most datasets.
claims.source: We also show that high FMOD transcript levels and hypomethylation of FMOD promoter are associated with poor prognosis in most datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 7A B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis of multiple publicly available GBM datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7A.

claims.claim: Hypomethylation of FMOD promoter is associated with poor prognosis in most datasets.
claims.source: We also show that high FMOD transcript levels and hypomethylation of FMOD promoter are associated with poor prognosis in most datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 7A B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis of multiple publicly available GBM datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7B.

claims.claim: AGR53-GSC-miRNT and AGR53-GSC-miRFMOD cell-initiated tumors show similar size 7 days after doxycycline treatment.
claims.source: AGR53-GSC/miRNT and AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cell-initiated tumors showed a similar size 7 days after doxycycline treatment as shown by mCherry fluorescence (Figure 5B and C; day 21).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence imaging data shown in Figures 5B and C.

claims.claim: Doxycycline administration significantly inhibits the growth of AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors over time but not that of AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors.
claims.source: However, upon subsequent follow-up, doxycycline administration significantly inhibited the growth of AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors over time but not that of AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors (Figure 5B, C and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence imaging and histology data shown in Figures 5B, C, and E.

claims.claim: Doxycycline administration increases the survival of mice injected with AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT cells.
claims.source: Further, doxycycline administration increased the survival of mice injected with AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT cells (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors show decreased FMOD, mCherry, and GFP expression compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT-initiated tumors.
claims.source: AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors showed decreased FMOD, mCherry, and GFP expression compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT-initiated tumors (Figure 5F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 5F and G.

claims.claim: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration in DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD cells results in reduced tumor growth.
claims.source: DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD, another murine glioma GSC cell line, produced similar results: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration resulted in reduced tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A B), increased mice survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and decreased FMOD expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence and fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration in DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD cells increases mice survival.
claims.source: DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD, another murine glioma GSC cell line, produced similar results: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration resulted in reduced tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A B), increased mice survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and decreased FMOD expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration in DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD cells decreases FMOD expression.
claims.source: DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD, another murine glioma GSC cell line, produced similar results: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration resulted in reduced tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A B), increased mice survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and decreased FMOD expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Higher expression of CD133 confirms the enrichment of CSCs in MGG8-GSC neurospheres compared to MGG8-DGCs.
claims.source: The higher expression of CD133 confirmed the enrichment of CSCs in MGG8-GSC neurospheres compared to MGG8-DGCs (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: MGG8-GSC/shNT-transplanted mice readily develop intracranial tumors, whereas MGG8-GSC/shFMOD mice show impaired tumor formation and increased mice survival.
claims.source: Reminiscent of results obtained using transplantation of murine glioma cells, MGG8-GSC/shNT-transplanted mice readily developed intracranial tumors, whereas MGG8-GSC/shFMOD mice showed impaired tumor formation and increased mice survival (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and histology data shown in Figures 6B and C.

claims.claim: MGG8-GSC/shNT tumors show high expression of FMOD, while FMOD is barely detectable in MGG8-GSC/shFMOD tumors.
claims.source: Immunostaining and confocal microscopy analysis showed high expression of FMOD in MGG8-GSC/shNT tumors, while FMOD was barely detectable in MGG8-GSC/shFMOD tumors (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: U251/shFMOD cells develop smaller tumors, and mice bearing U251/shFMOD tumors have longer survival than those carrying U251/shNT tumors.
claims.source: Likewise, U251/shFMOD cells that showed reduced FMOD protein levels compared to U251/shNT (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A) developed smaller tumors, and mice bearing U251/shFMOD tumors had longer survival than those carrying U251/shNT tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, and histology data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claims.claim: FMOD expression is more elevated in U251/shNT tumors than in U251/shFMOD tumors.
claims.source: As expected, the expression of FMOD was more elevated in U251/shNT tumors than in U251/shFMOD tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for the growth of both human and mouse glioma.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings indicate that DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for the growth of both human and mouse glioma.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple in vivo experiments showing FMOD silencing reduces tumor growth in both human and mouse glioma models.

claims.claim: CD133-positive cells are much less in proportion compared to GFAP-positive cells in tumors formed by AGR53-GSC, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs under FMOD nontargeting conditions.
claims.source: The CD133-positive cells are much less in proportion compared to GFAP-positive cells in tumors formed by AGR53-GSC, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs under FMOD nontargeting conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A B, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A B), in good correlation to the low proportion of GSCs seen in brain tumors (Singh et al., 2004; Galli et al., 2004; Calabrese et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and B, and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Most GFAP-positive cells are also positive for FMOD expression compared to CD133-positive cells in tumors.
claims.source: Further, most GFAP-positive cells are also positive for FMOD expression compared to CD133-positive cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A C, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A C), recapitulating the results we obtained in vitro, where FMOD is expressed specifically by DGCs (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization of FMOD with GFAP in tumor sections.

claims.claim: Similar expression pattern of CD133 and GFAP markers is found in small tumors formed under FMOD-silenced conditions in all three tumor models.
claims.source: We also found a similar expression pattern of CD133 and GFAP markers in small tumors formed under FMOD-silenced conditions in all three tumor models (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3D E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3D and E.

claims.claim: GFAP staining in tumors formed under FMOD-silenced conditions confirms the occurrence of an efficient differentiation program even in FMOD-silenced conditions.
claims.source: The GFAP staining in these tumors confirms the occurrence of an efficient differentiation program even in FMOD-silenced conditions, which confirms our results obtained in vitro, where the absence of FMOD failed to affect the GSC differentiation to form DGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from GFAP staining data in tumors and in vitro differentiation experiments.

claims.claim: Small tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions show substantially reduced FMOD staining.
claims.source: As expected, the small tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions showed substantially reduced FMOD staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3D F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3D and F.

claims.claim: Small size tumors formed by AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells after doxycycline treatment show reduced staining for CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF) compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors.
claims.source: The small size tumors formed by AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells after doxycycline treatment showed reduced staining for CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF) compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors (Figure 7A-C, Figure 7—figure supplement 4A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 7A-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 4A-C.

claims.claim: Tumors formed by DBT-Luc-GSC/miRFMOD cells in doxycycline-treated mice show significantly reduced CD31 staining compared to that measured in the absence of doxycycline treatment.
claims.source: Tumors formed by DBT-Luc-GSC/miRFMOD cells in doxycycline-treated mice also showed significantly reduced CD31 staining compared to that measured in the absence of doxycycline treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 4D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4D-F.

claims.claim: Tumors induced by MGG8-GSC/shFMOD cells show reduced CD31 staining compared to MGG8-GSC/shNT cells.
claims.source: Reminiscent of murine glioma tumors, tumors induced by MGG8-GSC/shFMOD cells also showed reduced CD31 staining compared to MGG8-GSC/shNT cells (Figure 7D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 7D-F.

claims.claim: In all three tumor models (AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs), blood vessels formed by TDECs are significantly reduced in tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions.
claims.source: We then tested the extent of blood vessel formation by TDECs. In all three tumor models (AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs), blood vessels formed by TDECs were significantly reduced in tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions (Figure 7G–L, Figure 7—figure supplement 4G–I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization of CD31 with GFP or GFAP in tumor sections, shown in Figures 7G-L and Figure 7—figure supplement 4G-I.

claims.claim: Confocal microscopy analysis in tumors formed by AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs reveals significant colocalization of the endothelial cell marker CD31 with FMOD, pFAK, JAG1, and HES1 markers in blood vessels.
claims.source: Next, we investigated the involvement of integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis in the context of glioma tumors. Confocal microscopy analysis in tumors formed by AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs revealed a significant colocalization of the endothelial cell marker CD31 with FMOD, pFAK, JAG1, and HES1 markers in blood vessels (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5A-C.

claims.claim: Angiogenesis induced by DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for glioma tumor growth.
claims.source: From these results, we conclude that angiogenesis induced by DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for glioma tumor growth.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing FMOD silencing reduces angiogenesis and tumor growth in vivo.

claims.claim: Tumor-initiating capacity lies solely with CSCs.
claims.source: It is well established that the tumor-initiating capacity lies solely with CSCs, thereby making them the crucial architects of tumor–stroma interactions that favor tumor growth and progression (Rheinbay et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Rheinbay et al., 2013.

claims.claim: CSCs are capable of self-renewal and give rise to differentiated cells that form the bulk of the tumor.
claims.source: CSCs have a dichotomous division pattern as they are capable of self-renewal and give rise to differentiated cells that form the bulk of the tumor (Olmeda and Ben Amar, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Olmeda and Ben Amar, 2019.

claims.claim: The indispensable role of CSCs is well documented in many solid tumors.
claims.source: The indispensable role of CSCs, which usually constitute only a minority population within tumors, is well documented in many solid tumors (Galli et al., 2004; Ignatova et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Galli et al., 2004; Ignatova et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2004; and Yang et al., 2020a.

claims.claim: The tumor microenvironment is a vital driver of plasticity and heterogeneity in cancer.
claims.source: The tumor microenvironment is a vital driver of plasticity and heterogeneity in cancer (Carnero and Lleonart, 2016; Heddleston et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Carnero and Lleonart, 2016 and Heddleston et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The presence of hypoxic and necrotic regions is the hallmark of very aggressive tumors like glioblastoma (GBM).
claims.source: The presence of hypoxic and necrotic regions is the hallmark of very aggressive tumors like glioblastoma (GBM), which have a highly vascular niche that supplies nutrients to cancer cells and makes a conducive environment for the tumor cells to thrive (Hambardzumyan and Bergers, 2015; Huang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Hambardzumyan and Bergers, 2015 and Huang et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Paracrine signaling mediated by proteins secreted from tumor cells, particularly glioma stem-like cells (GSCs), helps acquire a highly vascular phenotype by attracting blood vessels and inducing pro-angiogenic signaling in endothelial cells through extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling.
claims.source: Paracrine signaling mediated by proteins secreted from tumor cells, particularly glioma stem-like cells (GSCs), helps acquire this highly vascular phenotype by attracting blood vessels and inducing pro-angiogenic signaling in endothelial cells through extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling (Dittmer and Leyh, 2014; Rupp et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Dittmer and Leyh, 2014 and Rupp et al., 2016.

claims.claim: A reciprocal relationship exists between GSCs and endothelial cells by which endothelial cells induce stemness phenotype in cancer cells through activation of Notch, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and nitric oxide synthase signaling pathways.
claims.source: A reciprocal relationship exists between GSCs and endothelial cells by which endothelial cells induce stemness phenotype in cancer cells through activation of Notch, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and nitric oxide synthase signaling pathways (Jeon et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011), while GSCs drive vascularization of the tumor via endogenous endothelial cell stimulation, vascular mimicry, and GBM-endothelial cell transdifferentiation (Hardee and Zagzag, 2012; Soda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Jeon et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2014; and Zhu et al., 2011.

claims.claim: GSCs drive vascularization of the tumor via endogenous endothelial cell stimulation, vascular mimicry, and GBM-endothelial cell transdifferentiation.
claims.source: A reciprocal relationship exists between GSCs and endothelial cells by which endothelial cells induce stemness phenotype in cancer cells through activation of Notch, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and nitric oxide synthase signaling pathways (Jeon et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011), while GSCs drive vascularization of the tumor via endogenous endothelial cell stimulation, vascular mimicry, and GBM-endothelial cell transdifferentiation (Hardee and Zagzag, 2012; Soda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Hardee and Zagzag, 2012 and Soda et al., 2011.

claims.claim: CSCs induce high vascularization of tumors like GBM by migrating along blood vessel scaffolds to invade novel vascular niches.
claims.source: Recent reports have shown that CSCs induce high vascularization of tumors like GBM by migrating along blood vessel scaffolds to invade novel vascular niches, thereby ensuring surplus and continuous blood supply at their disposal (Prager et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Prager et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In GBM, CD133+ and Nestin+ cells (representing GSCs) are located in close proximity to the tumor microvascular density (MVD), whereas a lower number of CD133- and Nestin- cells (representing differentiated glioma cells [DGCs]) are located in the vicinity of the blood vessels.
claims.source: In GBM, CD133+ and Nestin+ cells (representing GSCs) are located in close proximity to the tumor microvascular density (MVD), whereas a lower number of CD133- and Nestin- cells (representing differentiated glioma cells [DGCs]) are located in the vicinity of the blood vessels.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge without a specific citation in this sentence, but is supported by the citation to Calabrese et al., 2007 in the next sentence.

claims.claim: Depletion of brain tumor blood vessels causes a decrease in the number of tumor-initiating GSCs.
claims.source: It has also been reported that the depletion of brain tumor blood vessels causes a decrease in the number of tumor-initiating GSCs (Calabrese et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Calabrese et al., 2007.

claims.claim: CD133 marker expression was initially reported to be associated with GSCs.
claims.source: While CD133 marker expression was reported to be associated with GSCs initially (Singh et al., 2004; Galli et al., 2004), later reports documented CD133- cells exhibiting GSC-like properties (Beier et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010; Joo et al., 2008; Ogden et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Singh et al., 2004 and Galli et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Later reports documented CD133- cells exhibiting GSC-like properties.
claims.source: While CD133 marker expression was reported to be associated with GSCs initially (Singh et al., 2004; Galli et al., 2004), later reports documented CD133- cells exhibiting GSC-like properties (Beier et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010; Joo et al., 2008; Ogden et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Beier et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010; Joo et al., 2008; Ogden et al., 2008; and Wang et al., 2008.

claims.claim: CXCR4-dependent SHH-GLI-NANOG signaling promotes stemness in GSCs.
claims.source: CXCR4-dependent SHH-GLI-NANOG signaling promotes stemness in GSCs. This study also showed that the miR302-367 cluster could suppress stemness and promote differentiation by targeting CXCR4/SDF1 (Fareh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Fareh et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The miR302-367 cluster can suppress stemness and promote differentiation by targeting CXCR4/SDF1.
claims.source: CXCR4-dependent SHH-GLI-NANOG signaling promotes stemness in GSCs. This study also showed that the miR302-367 cluster could suppress stemness and promote differentiation by targeting CXCR4/SDF1 (Fareh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Fareh et al., 2012.

claims.claim: miR18A* promotes GSC stemness by activating Notch-dependent SHH-GL1-NANOG signaling, targeting DLL3, an autocrine inhibitor of Notch 1 signaling.
claims.source: The above group subsequently showed that miR18A* promotes GSC stemness by activating Notch-dependent SHH-GL1-NANOG signaling, targeting DLL3, an autocrine inhibitor of Notch 1 signaling (Turchi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Turchi et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Dirkse et al. showed the existence of stem cell-associated heterogeneity in GBM, which results in tumor plasticity and is orchestrated by the microenvironment.
claims.source: In contrast to these observations, Dirkse et al. showed the existence of stem cell-associated heterogeneity in GBM, which results in tumor plasticity and is orchestrated by the microenvironment (Dirkse et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Dirkse et al., 2019.

claims.claim: CSC differentiation to form the bulk cancer cells plays a crucial role in tumor growth and maintenance.
claims.source: Besides CSC self-renewal, their differentiation to form the bulk cancer cells also plays a crucial role in tumor growth and maintenance (Jin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Jin et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Epigenome unique to CSCs compared to differentiated cancer cells has been documented.
claims.source: Epigenome unique to CSCs compared to differentiated cancer cells has been documented (Suvà et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Suvà et al., 2014 and Zhou et al., 2018.

claims.claim: A set of four reprogramming transcription factors, POU3F2, SOX2, SALL2, and OLIG2, is identified in GBM that is sufficient to reprogram DGCs and create the epigenetic landscape of native GSCs.
claims.source: Reciprocally, a set of four reprogramming transcription factors, POU3F2, SOX2, SALL2, and OLIG2, is identified in GBM that is sufficient to reprogram DGCs and create the epigenetic landscape of native GSCs, thus creating 'induced' CSCs (Suvà et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Suvà et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Epigenetic regulation forms the basis of cellular plasticity, which creates a dynamic equilibrium between CSCs and differentiated cancer cells.
claims.source: The epigenetic regulation forms the basis of cellular plasticity, which creates a dynamic equilibrium between CSCs and differentiated cancer cells (Safa et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Safa et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Oncogene-induced dedifferentiation of mature cells in the brain was reported using a mouse model of glioma.
claims.source: Oncogene-induced dedifferentiation of mature cells in the brain was also reported using a mouse model of glioma, and the reprogrammed CSCs were proposed to contribute to the heterogeneous cell state populations observed in malignant gliomas (Friedmann-Morvinski et al., 2012; Friedmann-Morvinski and Verma, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Friedmann-Morvinski et al., 2012 and Friedmann-Morvinski and Verma, 2014.

claims.claim: Reprogrammed CSCs contribute to the heterogeneous cell state populations observed in malignant gliomas.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Friedmann-Morvinski et al., 2012 and Friedmann-Morvinski and Verma, 2014.

results.result: Proteomic analysis reveals that FMOD is the most differentially abundant ECM proteoglycan in DGC versus GSC conditioned media. Quantitative mass spectrometry identified 185 proteins more abundant in DGC CM and 119 in GSC CM, with DGC CM enriched in extracellular/cell surface proteins. FMOD exhibited the highest DGC/GSC ratio among ECM proteoglycans and was validated at transcript and protein levels in multiple cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C12, C16-C17 provide converging proteomic, transcriptomic, and protein-level evidence across multiple independent cell lines (MGG4, MGG6, MGG8) using orthogonal methods (mass spec, RT-qPCR, Western blot). The statistical significance (p<0.05) and biological replication support the conclusion that FMOD is preferentially expressed by DGCs.

results.result: TGF-β signaling drives FMOD expression in DGCs through direct pSMAD2 binding to the FMOD promoter. GSEA shows TGF-β pathway enrichment in DGCs and GBM datasets. TGF-β inhibition (SB431542) reduces FMOD transcript/protein levels and promoter activity, while ChIP demonstrates pSMAD2 occupancy on the FMOD promoter that is inhibited by SB431542. DGCs also show mesenchymal enrichment consistent with elevated TGF-β/FMOD.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C32 establish a mechanistic link between TGF-β signaling and FMOD expression through multiple lines of evidence: GSEA pathway analysis, pharmacological inhibition, luciferase reporters, and direct ChIP demonstration of pSMAD2 binding. The consistency across methods and correlation with mesenchymal subtype strongly support this regulatory mechanism.

results.result: FMOD downregulation does not affect GSC growth, differentiation, or DGC growth and reprogramming in vitro. Neurosphere assays, limiting dilution assays, and differentiation/reprogramming experiments in multiple cell lines show no significant effects of FMOD silencing on these cellular processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 are supported by multiple functional assays (neurosphere formation, limiting dilution, differentiation markers) across multiple cell lines showing no significant differences. This negative result is important for establishing that FMOD's role is not in cell-autonomous growth or plasticity, directing focus to paracrine mechanisms.

results.result: DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for GSC-initiated tumor growth in vivo. Co-implantation experiments show that DGCs with silenced FMOD (miRFMOD + doxycycline) fail to support GSC tumor growth compared to control DGCs, with tumors remaining small and expressing low FMOD levels. GSCs alone or with FMOD-silenced DGCs form significantly smaller tumors than GSCs co-implanted with FMOD-expressing DGCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C33-C38 demonstrate through controlled co-implantation experiments with inducible FMOD silencing that DGC-derived FMOD is necessary for GSC tumor growth. The experimental design with doxycycline-inducible knockdown, multiple control groups, and quantitative bioluminescence measurements provides strong evidence for this paracrine requirement.

results.result: FMOD induces angiogenesis in endothelial cells through paracrine signaling. FMOD-overexpressing cells and recombinant FMOD (rhFMOD) promote angiogenic network formation, while FMOD silencing or neutralizing antibodies reduce angiogenesis. These effects are rescued by adding exogenous rhFMOD. FMOD induces endothelial cell migration and invasion but not proliferation, and promotes angiogenesis in multiple endothelial cell types including primary HBMECs and immortalized cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C53, C60-C61 provide comprehensive evidence through gain-of-function (overexpression, rhFMOD addition), loss-of-function (silencing, neutralizing antibodies), and rescue experiments across multiple endothelial cell types. The consistency of results and specificity of FMOD neutralization strongly support FMOD as a critical mediator of DGC-induced angiogenesis.

results.result: FMOD promotes vascular mimicry by inducing tumor-derived endothelial cells (TDECs) to form angiogenic networks. DGCs differentiate to TDECs (CD31+) under hypoxic conditions in endothelial media, with FMOD-silenced cells showing reduced TDEC formation. rhFMOD induces both control and FMOD-silenced TDECs to form angiogenic networks efficiently.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 demonstrate FMOD's role in vascular mimicry through TDEC differentiation assays and network formation assays. The use of hypoxic conditions and endothelial media to induce TDECs, combined with CD31 marker validation and functional network assays, provides solid evidence for this alternative angiogenic mechanism.

results.result: FMOD activates Notch signaling in endothelial cells to promote angiogenesis. RPPA identified HES1 (Notch target) upregulation in FMOD-treated cells. rhFMOD induces Notch reporter activity, HES1 expression, and NICD nuclear translocation, all blocked by gamma-secretase inhibitor (GSI). NICD overexpression enhances angiogenesis independently of FMOD, and GSI blocks FMOD-induced angiogenesis, establishing Notch activation as essential for FMOD's angiogenic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C70 establish Notch pathway involvement through multiple approaches: unbiased RPPA discovery, luciferase reporters, endogenous gene expression, subcellular localization, pharmacological inhibition, and genetic overexpression. The epistasis experiments (NICD overexpression bypassing FMOD requirement, GSI blocking FMOD effects) provide strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: FMOD activates integrin-FAK-Src signaling in endothelial cells. RPPA shows pFAK upregulation by rhFMOD. RGD peptide (integrin inhibitor) blocks FMOD-induced pFAK and angiogenesis. FAK and Src inhibitors completely block FMOD-induced angiogenesis, while inactive Src inhibitor (PP3) and ROCK/RAC1 inhibitors do not, indicating specificity for the integrin-FAK-Src axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 demonstrate integrin-FAK-Src pathway involvement through RPPA discovery, pharmacological inhibition with multiple specific inhibitors, and appropriate negative controls (PP3, ROCK, RAC1 inhibitors). The specificity of pathway inhibition and lack of effect from related but distinct pathways support this mechanism.

results.result: FMOD requires type I collagen binding and specific integrin heterodimers (αv/β1 and α6/β1) to activate integrin signaling. A synthetic peptide (RLDGNEIKR) corresponding to FMOD's 11th LRR that competes for collagen binding inhibits FMOD-induced Notch activation and angiogenesis, while a control peptide does not. Silencing ITGA6, ITGB1, or ITGAV reduces FMOD-induced pFAK, identifying the specific integrin receptors involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 establish the molecular mechanism of FMOD-integrin interaction through structure-based peptide competition (with appropriate negative control peptide) and genetic silencing of specific integrin subunits. The convergence of peptide competition and genetic approaches, combined with prior structural knowledge, strongly supports this mechanism.

results.result: JAG1 links integrin and Notch signaling in FMOD-treated endothelial cells through an integrin-FAK-KLF8-JAG1-Notch-HES1 pathway. FMOD induces JAG1 expression in an integrin-FAK-Src-dependent manner (blocked by RGD, FAKi, PP2 but not PP3). JAG1 silencing abolishes FMOD-induced Notch activation and angiogenesis. FMOD induces KLF8 (FAK-inducible transcription factor) in an integrin-dependent manner, and KLF8 silencing reduces JAG1 induction, establishing the complete signaling cascade.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C98 establish a complete signaling pathway through systematic pharmacological inhibition, genetic silencing at multiple nodes (JAG1, KLF8), and demonstration of epistatic relationships. The specificity of inhibitors (PP2 vs PP3), requirement for each pathway component, and rescue experiments provide strong mechanistic evidence for this integrin-Notch crosstalk.

results.result: FMOD, JAG1, and HES1 are upregulated and correlated in human GBM, and high FMOD expression/promoter hypomethylation associate with poor prognosis. Analysis of multiple GBM datasets shows significant upregulation of FMOD, JAG1, and HES1 transcripts, positive correlations between FMOD-HES1 and FMOD-JAG1 expression, and association of high FMOD levels or FMOD promoter hypomethylation with worse patient survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 validate the mechanistic findings in human disease through analysis of multiple independent patient datasets. The consistency across datasets, correlation between pathway components, and prognostic associations provide clinical relevance and support the biological significance of the FMOD-integrin-Notch pathway in human GBM.

results.result: Conditional FMOD silencing in DGCs generated in vivo from GSCs inhibits tumor growth and extends survival in murine glioma models. AGR53-GSC and DBT-Luc-GSC tumors with inducible FMOD knockdown (miRFMOD + doxycycline) show similar initial growth but significantly reduced growth after doxycycline administration, with decreased FMOD/mCherry/GFP expression and increased mouse survival compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C110 demonstrate therapeutic potential through temporally controlled FMOD silencing in established tumors using doxycycline-inducible systems. The experimental design allows tumors to establish from GSCs, then silences FMOD in newly differentiated DGCs, directly testing the hypothesis that DGC-derived FMOD is required for continued tumor growth. Results across two independent cell lines strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: FMOD silencing in human GSCs impairs tumor formation and extends survival in xenograft models. MGG8-GSCs with FMOD knockdown show impaired tumor formation and increased survival compared to control GSCs, with barely detectable FMOD in resulting tumors. U251 cells with FMOD knockdown also develop smaller tumors with longer survival and reduced FMOD expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C116 extend the murine findings to human cells through xenograft experiments. The use of CD133 to confirm GSC enrichment, survival analysis, histology, and FMOD immunostaining across two human cell lines (patient-derived MGG8 and established U251) provide strong evidence that FMOD's role is conserved in human glioma.

results.result: Tumors maintain normal GSC/DGC proportions and differentiation capacity under FMOD-silenced conditions. CD133+ cells are proportionally less abundant than GFAP+ cells in all tumor models regardless of FMOD status. GFAP+ cells predominantly express FMOD compared to CD133+ cells. FMOD-silenced tumors show similar CD133/GFAP marker patterns and GFAP staining confirms efficient differentiation occurs even without FMOD.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 address a critical control: demonstrating that reduced tumor growth in FMOD-silenced conditions is not due to impaired GSC differentiation. The immunofluorescence analysis across three tumor models showing maintained differentiation markers and normal GSC/DGC proportions, consistent with in vitro findings (C3-C4), supports that FMOD's role is specifically in supporting tumor growth through paracrine mechanisms rather than affecting cellular differentiation.

results.result: FMOD-silenced tumors show reduced angiogenesis from host-derived endothelial cells. Tumors from FMOD-silenced cells (AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD, DBT-Luc-GSC/miRFMOD, MGG8-GSC/shFMOD) show significantly reduced CD31 and von Willebrand factor staining compared to controls, indicating decreased blood vessel formation across multiple tumor models.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 demonstrate the in vivo consequence of FMOD silencing on angiogenesis through quantitative immunofluorescence of endothelial markers (CD31, vWF) across three independent tumor models (two murine, one human xenograft). The consistency across models and use of multiple endothelial markers provide strong evidence that reduced tumor growth correlates with impaired angiogenesis.

results.result: FMOD-silenced tumors show reduced vascular mimicry (tumor-derived endothelial cells) and the integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 pathway is active in tumor blood vessels. Blood vessels formed by TDECs (CD31+/GFP+ or CD31+/GFAP+) are significantly reduced in FMOD-silenced tumors across all three models. Confocal microscopy shows colocalization of CD31 with FMOD, pFAK, JAG1, and HES1 in blood vessels of control tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 demonstrate that FMOD affects both conventional angiogenesis and vascular mimicry in vivo, and validate that the mechanistic pathway identified in vitro (integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1) is active in actual tumor blood vessels. The colocalization studies provide spatial evidence linking FMOD to pathway activation in the relevant cellular compartment (endothelium).

results.result: Angiogenesis induced by DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for glioma tumor growth. This conclusion integrates findings that FMOD silencing reduces both host-derived and tumor-derived angiogenesis in vivo, correlating with reduced tumor growth, while not affecting GSC differentiation or intrinsic growth properties.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 represents the central conclusion synthesizing multiple lines of evidence: (1) FMOD is DGC-specific, (2) FMOD induces angiogenesis in vitro, (3) FMOD silencing reduces tumor angiogenesis in vivo, (4) FMOD silencing reduces tumor growth without affecting differentiation, and (5) the mechanism involves integrin-Notch signaling in endothelial cells. The convergence of these findings strongly supports this integrative conclusion.

results.result: Background literature establishes the importance of CSCs, tumor microenvironment, angiogenesis, and cellular plasticity in glioma. Prior work demonstrates CSC tumor-initiating capacity, CSC-endothelial cell reciprocal interactions, GSC-driven angiogenesis, CD133 as a GSC marker (with caveats), epigenetic regulation of CSC/DGC plasticity, and recent evidence for DGC-GSC cooperation through neurotrophin signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C155 represent cited prior work that establishes the scientific context. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to peer-reviewed literature. While the authors should be credited for accurately representing prior work, these claims represent established knowledge rather than novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work based on the claims made.
